DURR-FULL:v2p394/r6.claim: The obedient wealthy person's wealth accompanies him over the bridge and tells him to proceed because he paid God's due.

DURR-FULL:v2p395/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p395/r1.speaker: أبو الدرداء
DURR-FULL:v2p395/r1.claim: By contrast, disobedient wealth rides on its owner's shoulders over the bridge, lamenting that he did not pay God's due.

DURR-FULL:v2p395/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p395/r2.speaker: مسروق
DURR-FULL:v2p395/r2.claim: A man who withholds relatives' rights from his wealth will have it become a snake around his neck saying it is his wealth.

DURR-FULL:v2p395/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p395/r3.speaker: إبراهيم النخعي
DURR-FULL:v2p395/r3.claim: The wealth withheld becomes a collar of fire.

DURR-FULL:v2p395/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p395/r4.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v2p395/r4.claim: They will be burdened at resurrection to produce the equivalent of the wealth they withheld.

BURSEVI:v2p107#3/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v2p107#3/r1.speaker: بعض الكبار
BURSEVI:v2p107#3/r1.claim: A saying attributed to one of the great elders says a trial reveals whether a person is honored or disgraced.

BURSEVI:v2p107#3/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v2p107#3/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v2p107#3/r2.claim: The grammatical object of ‘do not think’ is omitted but supplied by ‘their stinginess’: stinginess is not better than spending and is worse because it brings punishment.

BURSEVI:v2p107#3/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v2p107#3/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v2p107#3/r3.claim: The collar is a representative metaphor for the unavoidable burden and sin of stinginess; another view takes it literally as a snake or fiery collar, with a hadith to follow.

BURSEVI:v2p107#3/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v2p107#3/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v2p107#3/r4.claim: The heavens and earth belong to God alone; people should not withhold wealth from its owner, and what they keep remains behind at death with regret.

BURSEVI:v2p107#3/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v2p107#3/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v2p107#3/r5.claim: God knows both withholding and giving and recompenses them.

BURSEVI:v2p107#3/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v2p107#3/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v2p107#3/r6.claim: Bukh means refusing a duty, not declining optional charity; duties include supporting oneself and dependents, famine relief, and needed military aid.

BURSEVI:v2p107#3/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v2p107#3/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v2p107#3/r7.claim: Spiritually, stinginess turns God's gift into misery, while generosity makes it a blessing leading to happiness and Paradise.

BURSEVI:v2p107#3/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v2p107#3/r8.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v2p107#3/r8.claim: Love of wealth is like a collar around the heart and breeds miserliness, greed, envy, rancor, hostility, pride, anger, and other vices.

BURSEVI:v2p107#3/r9.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v2p107#3/r9.speaker: النبي
BURSEVI:v2p107#3/r9.claim: The Prophet calls love of this world the root of every sin; withholding zakat wraps the luminous spirit in low, dark traits and their veils.

BURSEVI:v2p108/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v2p108/r1.speaker: رسول الله
BURSEVI:v2p108/r1.claim: The Prophet says a person who fails to pay zakat will wear a bald serpent with two dark marks as a collar; it grips his jaws, identifies itself as his wealth, and the Prophet recites this verse.

BURSEVI:v2p108/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v2p108/r2.speaker: رسول الله
BURSEVI:v2p108/r2.claim: A second report says withheld zakat becomes a snake around the neck that bites from head to foot and pecks the head, saying it is the owner's wealth.

BURSEVI:v2p108/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v2p108/r3.speaker: رسول الله
BURSEVI:v2p108/r3.claim: Those who withhold the due on livestock will be trampled and gored by their animals repeatedly until judgment is completed.

BURSEVI:v2p108/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v2p108/r4.speaker: أبو حامد
BURSEVI:v2p108/r4.claim: Abū Ḥāmid describes the withheld due as an enormous camel, bull, sheep, grain sacks, or heavy snake carried on the owner's shoulders while angels identify it as what he hoarded.

BURSEVI:v2p108/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v2p108/r5.speaker: رسول الله
BURSEVI:v2p108/r5.claim: The Prophet says zakat protects wealth, charity treats illness, and supplication meets calamities; he also says prayer is invalid without zakat.

BURSEVI:v2p108/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v2p108/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v2p108/r6.claim: Moses admires a man's focused prayer, but God says even vast prayer, emancipation, funerals, pilgrimage, and campaigns are useless until zakat is paid.

BURSEVI:v2p108/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v2p108/r7.speaker: رسول الله
BURSEVI:v2p108/r7.claim: The Prophet calls wealth without annual zakat and a body never tested within forty nights accursed; trials include falls, illness, scratches, and eye twitching.

BURSEVI:v2p108/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v2p108/r8.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v2p108/r8.claim: These reports show the burden of persistent refusal to pay zakat freely and with a willing heart, even after wealth and circumstances favor the owner.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p139#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p139#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p139#2/r1.claim: The verse says what they hoard is evil for them, then explains the evil through their being encircled by it on Judgment Day; the extra sīn intensifies the threat.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p139#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p139#2/r2.speaker: أبو هريرة
ALUSI-FULL:v4p139#2/r2.claim: A hadith in al-Bukhārī says that one who fails to pay zakat on divinely granted wealth will meet a bald two-marked snake that coils around him, grips his jaw, and says it is his wealth and treasure.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p139#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p139#2/r3.speaker: النبي
ALUSI-FULL:v4p139#2/r3.claim: Another prophetic report says a relative who refuses a petitioner from God’s bounty will meet a hellish snake on Judgment Day that licks its lips and coils around him.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p139#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p139#2/r4.speaker: إبراهيم النخعي
ALUSI-FULL:v4p139#2/r4.claim: Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī says the hoarded wealth itself will become a collar of fire around the hoarder’s neck.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p139#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p139#2/r5.speaker: مجاهد
ALUSI-FULL:v4p139#2/r5.claim: Mujāhid interprets the threat as forcing misers to produce an equal sum on Judgment Day, which they will be unable to do.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p139#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p139#2/r6.speaker: أبو مسلم
ALUSI-FULL:v4p139#2/r6.claim: Abū Muslim reads it figuratively: they will bear the consequence of their miserliness like a collar, with a deleted ‘consequence’ implied.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p139#2/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p139#2/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p139#2/r7.claim: The apparent literal warning is the majority position and the verse apparently concerns those withholding zakat, as reports from al-Ṣādiq, Ibn Masʿūd, al-Shaʿbī, al-Suddī, and others indicate.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p139#2/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p139#2/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v4p139#2/r8.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās’s report says the verse concerns People of the Book who concealed the Torah’s description and prophecy of Muḥammad; their withheld bounty is the Torah, and the collar may be fire or the consequence of concealment.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p139/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p139/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p139/r1.claim: The verse corrects the miser’s belief that hoarding is good and follows the preceding warning about being allowed respite; alternatively it continues the call to give lives by urging giving wealth.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p139/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p139/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p139/r2.claim: Describing the hoarded wealth as God’s gift magnifies the wrong: receiving it from divine bounty should prompt its use in God’s cause.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p139/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p139/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p139/r3.claim: The first object of ḥasiba is omitted though the verb seeks two objects; an objection says its double grammatical demand should prevent deletion, but deletion of kāna’s predicate shows that inference fails.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p139/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p139/r4.speaker: الزمخشري
ALUSI-FULL:v4p139/r4.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī permits omitting an object of ḥasiba only when subject and objects are semantically one; the author rejects this as the governing rule and says contextual indication is decisive.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p139/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p139/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p139/r5.claim: Object omission depends on a clear contextual clue: it is allowed where indicated and not where it is absent, regardless of semantic identity.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p139/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p139/r6.speaker: عصام الدين، أبو البقاء
ALUSI-FULL:v4p139/r6.claim: A proposed parse treats huwa as an accusative pronoun or emphatic pronoun, but the author calls it strained and cites al-Durr al-Maṣūn calling that analysis an error.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p139/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p139/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p139/r7.claim: The author instead takes huwa as a separator between the two objects of ḥasiba; the alternative addressed reading requires the first object to mean the hoarding of those who withhold zakat.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p139/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p139/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p139/r8.claim: On the addressed reading, the first object is the relative phrase understood as their hoarding of what God gave, and the second is ‘good’; an omitted genitive is needed.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p140/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p140/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p140/r1.claim: On the People of the Book interpretation, the passage returns to the discussion leading into the Battle of Uḥud; many later verses in the sūra also concern them.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p140/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p140/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p140/r2.claim: God alone inherits all transferable possessions and states in heaven and earth, including prophetic missions; therefore misers withhold from the true owner what belongs to Him.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p140/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p140/r3.speaker: الزجاج
ALUSI-FULL:v4p140/r3.claim: Al-Zajjāj explains the inheritance literally: God ends the inhabitants’ lives, leaving heaven and earth and all they contain without another owner.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p140/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p140/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p140/r4.claim: God knows their withholding and miserliness; naming Him directly builds awe, while shifting to direct address intensifies the threat; Nāfiʿ and others read second-person, the rest third-person.

ELMALILI:3:180/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:3:180/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:3:180/r1.claim: The inheritance of the heavens and earth belongs solely to God: human heirs possess only temporary, borrowed holdings that perish, while God’s ownership remains.

ELMALILI:3:180/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:3:180/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:3:180/r2.claim: Those who hoard wealth and refuse to spend in God’s path should remember that they are withholding what belongs to its true owner and committing a grave sin.

ELMALILI:3:180/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:3:180/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:3:180/r3.claim: Heavenly inheritance also includes lofty gifts such as prophethood and knowledge; the verse prepares for the inheritance laws in the following Surah al-Nisa.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p181/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p181/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p181/r1.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī calls هو a separator pronoun, but al-Zajjāj, as quoted by al-Ṭībī, restricts separator pronouns to subject-predicate constructions; Abū al-Baqāʾ instead treats it as the first object, with nominative replacing accusative.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p181/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p181/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p181/r2.claim: The pronoun refers to stinginess inferred from يبخلون, as in the statement that justice is nearer to piety; when read as a separator, one object of حساب is omitted, with its wording depending on the recitation.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p181/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p181/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p181/r3.claim: Bukhl is withholding money without compensation; withholding non-monetary things is metaphorical. The word has regional vowel variants, and the Qurʾān uses the non-Ḥijāzī pattern; a prophetic report calls one who withholds blessings upon the Prophet a miser.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p182/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p182/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p182/r1.claim: The phrase بل هو شر لهم reinforces that stinginess is not good and rules out an imagined middle ground between good and evil, a familiar Arabic rhetorical pattern illustrated by Imruʾ al-Qays.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p182/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p182/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p182/r2.claim: سيطوقون may mean they will bear what they withheld as a burden beyond capacity, but more likely it means their wealth will become collars around their necks as punishment; either way the shame is exposed before the gathering.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p182/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p182/r3.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p182/r3.claim: The Prophet warns that whoever wrongfully takes a handspan of land will have it placed around his neck from seven earths on the Day of Resurrection.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p182/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p182/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p182/r4.claim: God's inheritance of heaven and earth reminds misers that wealth belongs to Him and everyone leaves it behind; His enduring ownership and knowledge make the passage warning, threat, and promise.

TABATABAI:3:180/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:3:180/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:3:180/r1.claim: As 16:97 suggests, faith is the spirit and source of the good life, while keeping that life active until its effects appear requires righteous deeds, just as bodily life requires functioning organs.

TABATABAI:3:180/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:3:180/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:3:180/r2.claim: The divine name is repeated, with the last three instances replacing pronouns, to emphasize God as the source of matters only His divinity can enact: testing, knowing the unseen, choosing messengers, and making faith possible.

TABATABAI:3:180/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:3:180/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:3:180/r3.claim: Following God's reprieve of disbelievers, the discussion turns to misers who rejoice and boast over wealth; calling it God's bounty highlights why their stinginess deserves blame, and being collared explains why it harms them.

TABATABAI:3:180/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:3:180/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:3:180/r4.claim: The phrase about God's inheritance of the heavens and earth is apparently circumstantial of the Day of Resurrection, as is God's knowledge of their deeds; alternatively, less likely, both relate to the misers or the final clause is independent.

TABATABAI:3:180/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:3:180/r5.speaker: أبو جعفر عليه السلام
TABATABAI:3:180/r5.claim: Asked whether death is better for an unbeliever or life, al-Bāqir says death is better for both believer and unbeliever, citing God's reward for the righteous and the warning that the reprieve of disbelievers is not good.

TABATABAI:3:180/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:3:180/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:3:180/r6.claim: The report's proof does not fully match the Imams' approach because the 'righteous' are a special class, not all believers, unless the term includes every believer's measure of righteousness; al-Durr reports the same sense from Ibn Masʿūd.

ASAD-NOTES:3:180#n138/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:3:180#n138/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:3:180#n138/r1.claim: The warning alludes to the unbelievers' way of life in verse 179: material attachment grounded in disbelief in anything beyond life's practical concerns.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:180/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:180/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:180/r1.claim: Some interpret the condemned withholding as metaphorical concealment of knowledge and truth by People of the Book who knew Muhammad's traits and prophethood; the stronger view concerns withholding wealth from jihad or zakat.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:180/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:180/r2.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:180/r2.claim: Miserliness humiliates people in this life and the next and is socially degrading; the Prophet called miserliness and cowardice the worst demeaning traits.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:180/r3.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:180/r3.speaker: İmam Mâverdî
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:180/r3.claim: Al-Mawardi says miserliness is a principal cause of injustice, friction, and conflict and a leading trait that lowers a person in others' eyes.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:180/r4.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:180/r4.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:180/r4.claim: Withholding God's gifts from the poor harms the miser morally and psychologically, can trouble conscience and trigger social upheaval, and brings punishment in the afterlife.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:180/r5.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:180/r5.speaker: Hz. Peygamber
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:180/r5.claim: The Prophet says unpaid zakat turns a miser's wealth into a venomous snake with dark marks that coils around and bites its owner's jaw, declaring itself his wealth and treasure; he then recited this verse.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:180/r6.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:180/r6.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:180/r6.claim: God owns the heavens, earth, and wealth; people are temporary custodians who inherit possessions from one another, while lasting ownership and inheritance belong to God.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:180/r7.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:180/r7.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:180/r7.claim: People should spend wealth where its true owner directs; money cannot be carried into the afterlife, but the reward of properly spent wealth can, and God knows each person's actions and purposes.

QIRAAT-ER:3:180:3#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:3:180:3#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:3:180:3#1/r1.claim: Kasra on sīn rather than fatḥa is a dialectal Form I imperfect variant with identical meaning.

QIRAAT-ER:3:180:3#2/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:3:180:3#2/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:3:180:3#2/r1.claim: The second-person address directs the warning to the Prophet and makes the hoarders the object of reckoning.

QIRAAT-ER:3:180:38#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:3:180:38#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:3:180:38#1/r1.claim: The third-person plural shifts from direct address to reference about the hoarders or people generally.

STUDYQURAN:3:180/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:3:180/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:3:180/r1.claim: The warning is interpreted as applying to the hoarding of both material wealth and spiritual knowledge.

STUDYQURAN:3:180/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:3:180/r2.speaker: Ṭ
STUDYQURAN:3:180/r2.claim: Ṭ identifies those withholding spiritual knowledge as the People of the Book, who refused to teach the scripture they possessed.

STUDYQURAN:3:180/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:3:180/r3.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:3:180/r3.claim: The image of being collared by what one withheld resembles the warning about fraud in 3:161.

STUDYQURAN:3:180/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:3:180/r4.speaker: the Prophet
STUDYQURAN:3:180/r4.claim: A report attributed to the Prophet says a miser's hoard appears at Judgment as a serpent that consumes or coils around him and identifies itself as his wealth and treasure; no grading is stated.

STUDYQURAN:3:180/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:3:180/r5.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:3:180/r5.claim: The harmful effects of miserliness are also treated in 4:37, 47:37–38, and 57:24.

STUDYQURAN:3:180/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:3:180/r6.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:3:180/r6.claim: The verse's conclusion resembles 19:40, where God says He will inherit the earth and all upon it.

STUDYQURAN:3:180/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:3:180/r7.speaker: Q, R, Ṭ
STUDYQURAN:3:180/r7.claim: Commentators distinguish God's inheritance from human inheritance: God always possesses the heavens and earth, and inherits them when all other owners cease to exist and He alone remains.
